newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Jobs creation proposal gains ground in EU talks.
newsitem.headline: Jobs creation proposal gains ground in EU talks.

text.p: Sweden put forward a detailed proposal on Tuesday on how the EU should step up efforts to fight unemployment amid continued scepticism over the idea among heavyweights Britain, Germany and France.
Denmark, Belgium and Austria have previously presented their own proposals on a special employment chapter in the treaty of the 15-nation European Union.

"With an employment chapter, we know that the fight against unemployment will always top the EU's agenda," said Gunnar Lund, Sweden's chief negotiator at the inter-governmental conference (IGC) which is reforming the EU and its institutions.

All member states agree that lowering an unemployment rate of some 11 percent, more than twice that in the United States, is a key priority. But there are different views on what role the EU should play.
Lund said a "large majority" were now in favour of an employment chapter in the treaty, which would legally bind the EU to consider job creation.
"There are still countries which are not deligthed with the idea," he told reporters on the second day of the two-day talks.
But he said there seemed now to be a clearly more open attitude from France and Germany.
A background paper from the Irish EU presidency confirmed that most countries were in favour of introducing "suitably formulated new provisions" on employment in the treaty.
However, it added: "Others are opposed to this."
According to the Swedish proposal, EU countries would commit themselves to a policy which promotes "a high and sustainable level of employment and low unemployment."
Each country would adopt multi-year employment programmes and the EU would monitor the developments in each member state.
In the case when a country's employment policies were not in line with EU objectives, EU ministers may "make the necessary recommendations to the member state concerned."
Lund said the issue would be discussed by EU foreign ministers when they meet next week in Luxembourg.
He stressed that the proposal in no way would interfere with plans to create a single currency in 1999 as feared by some, or automatically lead to more spending.
Employment policies would remain mainly a national responsibility, he added.
To promote coordination of national policies, a special employment committee with representatives from each member state would be set up to review the employment situation.
